content.intro: This lesson develops topic 79 of the supplied curriculum: **Broadcasting Rules**. The main starting point is **Aligning dimensions from the right**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Broadcasting allows compatible shapes to operate without explicitly copying repeated values. Reason about the dimensions from the rightmost side before changing the arrays.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Broadcasting Rules** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Aligning dimensions from the right** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print((a + b).shape)

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Broadcasting compares dimensions from the right. A pair of dimensions is compatible when the lengths match or either length is one; otherwise the operation raises `ValueError`.

common_mistakes.why: Broadcasting compares dimensions from the right.
common_mistakes.fix: Write the shapes side by side and align their rightmost dimensions.

common_mistakes.why: Explicit tiling can allocate extra memory.
common_mistakes.fix: Try broadcasting with singleton dimensions first.
